content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidance for the transport of infectious substances for the years 2023–2024. The guidance is intended for all stakeholders involved in the shipping process, including shippers, packaging suppliers, carriers, and receivers. It reflects changes in international regulatory frameworks and replaces the previous edition issued in 2021. Users are advised to consult applicable national and international regulations when using this document. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of technical experts, including Lisa Stevens, Rica Zinsky, and Markus Huber, in the development of this guidance. The production and technical editing were led by Kazunobu Kojima, with input from external experts such as Monika Gsell Albert and Katherine Rooney. The document emphasizes the importance of biosafety and biosecurity in the handling and transport of biological agents, which play a critical role in detecting and preventing outbreaks of infectious diseases. The UN Model Regulations, developed by the United Nations Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (UNCETDG), serve as a widely recognized framework for the safe transport of dangerous goods, including infectious substances. These regulations are continuously updated to reflect technical advancements, new materials, and emerging safety requirements. They provide a harmonized set of provisions that can be adapted to local needs and are often adopted as mandatory regulations by governments and international organizations. In addition to the UN Model Regulations, other international agreements and guidelines play a key role in the transport of infectious substances. For example, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) publishes legally binding Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air, which are applicable to all international flights. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) also publishes Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR), which incorporate ICAO provisions and may include additional restrictions. For rail transport, the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Rail (RID) regulations apply in Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. Road transport is governed by the Agreement concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Road (ADR), while sea transport follows the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code. Postal services, governed by the Universal Postal Union (UPU), may accept certain low-risk infectious substances but generally prohibit high-risk materials. Regional and subregional regulations, such as those in the European Union, address specific elements of infectious substance transport, including the management of animal by-products and pathogens. National regulations may adopt or modify international frameworks to suit local conditions, and the most stringent regulations should be applied when multiple frameworks are involved. Operator and carrier variations, such as those enforced by airlines or couriers, may impose additional safety requirements beyond legal regulations. Failure to comply with these variations can result in delays or refusal of service. Customs and border control agencies play a vital role in regulating the import and export of infectious substances. They often require specialized documentation, permits, and compliance with international safety standards. Harmonized System (HS) codes and Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) codes are essential for categorizing goods and ensuring streamlined customs processes. Dual-use items, which have both civilian and potential military applications, are subject to strict controls to prevent unauthorized access. Exporting such materials typically requires obtaining a license from the appropriate government authority.
